§ 2Content

§ 3The Mughal Empire

Babur (1526 AD–1530 AD)

  • Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodhi in the 1st Battle of Panipat on April 21, 1526 AD and was the founder of Mughal Dynasty.
  • Original name: Zahiruddin Muhammad Babur.
  • Title assumed: Padshah.
  • Babur was from Uzbekistan and considered himself descendant of Timur (from father's side) and Genghis Khan (from mother's side).
  • When he was 12 years old, he became the ruler of Ferghana in 1494.
  • He was forced to leave his throne after the Uzbegs, another Mongol group, invaded.
  • He conquered Kabul in 1504 AD.
  • In battles, he was the first to use gun powder massively.

Battles of Babur

  • 1526: 1st Battle of Panipat.
  • 1527: Battle of Khanwa (he defeated Rana Sanga of Mewar at Khanwa).
  • 1528: Battle of Chanderi (he defeated Medini Rai of Chanderi).
  • 1529: Battle of Ghaghra (he defeated Afghans (Mahmud Lodi)).
  • 1530: He died at Agra, where his tomb was initially placed but now it is located in Kabul.

Autobiography of Babur

  • Tuzuk-i-Baburi in Turkish.
  • It is translated in Persian language, named → Baburnama by Abdur Rahim Khanekhana.
  • It is translated in English by Madam Beveridge.

Architecture built by Babur

Humayun (1530 AD–1540 AD and 1555 AD–1556 AD)

  • He was the eldest son of Babur.
  • He ascended the throne in 1530 AD.
  • His succession was challenged by his brothers: Kamran, Hindal, Askari and Afghans as well.
  • Humayun's brother Kamran controlled Afghanistan and Punjab regions.
  • He fought two battles against Sher Shah Suri (Afghani ruler) at Chausa in 1539 AD and at Kannauj/Bilgram in 1540 AD, where he was completely defeated by Sher Shah.
  • Humayun after loosing battle took refuge at Safavid Dynasty (Iran).
  • His sister Gulbadan Begum, wrote his biography "Humayunnama".
  • After Sher Shah's death, Humayun regained his empire in 1555 AD.
  • He built Din Panah at Delhi as his 2nd capital.
  • He died in 1556 AD after falling from the stairs of his library.

Sher Shah Suri (1540 AD–1545 AD)

  • Original name: Farid Khan.
  • He was the son of Hasan Khan, the Jagirdar of Sasaram (Bihar).
  • Ibrahim Lodhi transferred his father's Jagir to him.

Battles of Sher Shah Suri:

  • 1539 AD: He defeated Humayun in Battle of Chausa and then assumed the title "Sher Shah".
  • 1540 AD: He defeated Humayun in Battle of Kannauj/Bilgram and annexed Kannauj under him.
  • He introduced Rupia as coin and fixed standard weights and measures all over the empire.
  • He built: Grand Trunk Road (runs from Chittagong (Bangladesh) to Peshwar).
  • Land revenue system: He started a land revenue system where the land was measured and 1/3rd of the average land was fixed as land tax. The peasants was given Patta (title deed) and a Qabuliyat (deed of agreement) which had fixed peasants rights and taxes.
  • Zamindars were removed and taxes collected directly.
  • Death: In 1545 AD, while conquering Kalinjar.
  • Buried in: Sasaram (Bihar).
  • He built Purana Quila at Delhi.

Sarai were shelters that provided food, water, and lodging for travelers while travelling through the GT Road.

Akbar (1556 AD–1605 AD)

  • One of the greatest ruler of Mughal Dynasty.
  • Eldest son of Humayun.
  • Full name: Abu'l-Fath Jalal-ud-din Muhammad Akbar.
  • Akbar ascended the throne at the age of 13 at Kalanaur, Punjab.
  • Regent: His tutor → Bairam Khan led Akbar's forces to victory in the 2nd Battle of Panipat in 1556 which was fought between him and Hemu (the Hindu General of Muhammad Adil Shah). Hemu was defeated, captured and slain.
  • Akbar tried to win over the Rajputas wherever possible and inducted Rajput kings into Mughal service and treated them at par with Mughal nobility.

Mughal Empire (continued)

  • Married: Harka Bai/Jodha Bai (daughter of Bharmal → Kachhwaha Rajput ruler of Amer). She was later honoured with title "Mariam-uz-Zamani" after she gave birth to Jahangir.
  • Rana Pratap Singh and son Amar Singh (Sisodiya Rajputs of Mewar, Capital: Chittor) did not recognize his supremacy.
  • This resulted in:
  • Battle of Haldighati (1576): Between Rana Pratap and Mughal army led by Man Singh of Amer. Rana Pratap was defeated but he never surrendered.
  • New religion proclaimed by Akbar: Din-i-Ilahi (1581), it was based on a synthesis of values and teachings from various religions, including Islam, Hinduism, Jainism, Christianity, and Zoroastrianism. Only Hindu to follow this religion was Birbal.

Architecture Built by Akbar

  • He built Fatehpur Sikri in 1570 AD in honour of Salim Chisti (a Sufi saint) and shifted his court from Agra to here.
  • Agra Fort (1565 AD)
  • Lahore Fort (1566 AD)
  • Buland Darwaja at Fatehpur Sikri (1573 AD) to commemorate his victory over Gujarat expedition.
  • Allahabad Fort (1585 AD)

Chronology of Akbar's capital shifts:

  • 1569 AD: Akbar's son Jahangir was born.
  • 1571 AD: Akbar shifted capital from Agra to Sikri.
  • 1585 AD: Capital shifted from Sikri to Lahore.
  • 1598 AD: Capital shifted from Lahore to Agra.

Navratnas of Akbar (Nine Jewels)

  1. 1. Birbal (Administrator)
  2. 2. Abul Fazal (Scholar and Statesman)
  3. 3. Faizi: Brother of Abul Fazal (Scholar and Statesman)
  4. 4. Tordarmal (Finance Minister, Dahsala Bandobast/Zabti)
  5. 5. Fakir Aziao-Din
  6. 6. Man Singh (Mansabdar, Grandson of Bharmal)
  7. 7. Tansen (Musician)
  8. 8. Abdul Rahim Khanekhana (Statesman, Hindi poet)
  9. 9. Mulla Do Pyaja

Charbagh Style of architecture was introduced by Mughals in India.

  • Akbar started Ibadatkhana (religious discussion used to happen here).

Tansen originally served under Raja Ramchandra Singh (Tomar Dynasty, ruling in Gwalior). Tansen's original name is Ramtanu Pande and he belonged to Rewa/Gwalior Gharana. He composed Dhrupads and played Rudraveena (Rabab). He was also given "Miyan" title by Akbar.

  • Abul Fazal wrote Akbarnama (Biography of Akbar) that has three parts:
  • 1st: It is about ancestors of Akbar.
  • 2nd: It is about reign of Akbar.
  • 3rd: Ain-i-Akbari (it is about his administration which was inspired from Sher Shah Suri).
  • Akbar also built a Translation Department (Maktab Khana).
  • Ramayana was translated into Persian by Abdul Qadir Badaiyuni.
  • Mahabharata was translated into Persian by Faizi and Abdul Qadir and was called "Razmnama".
  • Lilavati (by Bhaskaracharya) was converted to Persian by Faizi.

Land Revenue System

  • Revenue was fixed based on the average yield of the land over the past 10 years estimates known as Dahsala, also known as Zabti system. It was introduced by Todar Mal.
  1. 1. Polaj: The most fertile and productive land, cultivated regularly without being left fallow.
  2. 2. Parauti: Land left uncultivated for 1-2 years to regain its fertility.
  3. 3. Chachar: Land left fallow for 3-4 years before being cultivated again.
  4. 4. Banjar: Land that remained uncultivated for 5 years or more.
  • He abolished Jizya.

Administration

  • He started Mansabdari system in 1571. The word Mansab means rank or position which determined the status, salary and number of soldiers. Mansabdars were required to maintain:
  • Mansabs were graded on a numerical scale, with lowest rank being 10 and highest reaching 5000 (later raised to 7000 and 10,000).
  • Each Mansabs were assigned Zat, representing their personal rank.
  • Mansabdars were often payed in Jagirs (land assignments) from where they had the right to collect revenue from those lands.
  • Military commanders in Akbar's empire: Faujdars.
  • Raja Man Singh had a Mansab of 7000 (Sapth Hajari).

Last Expedition of Akbar

  • Akbar defeated Meeran Bahadur, ruler of Khandesh.
  • In 1601, Akbar carried out his last expedition in Fort of Asergarh of Khandesh (part of Ahmednagar). Akbar won, however his son Jahangir revolted against him.
  • He died in: 1605 → Tomb of Akbar in Sikandra, Agra.

Jahangir (1605 AD–1627 AD)

  • Original name: Nur-ud-Din Muhammad Salim/Prince Salim.
  • Established: Zanjir-i-Adal (i.e. Chain of Justice) at Agra Fort for seekers of royal justice. Jahangir was known for his strict administration of justice.
  • In 1611 AD, he married Mehr-un-Nissa (widow of Sher Afghan, a Persian nobleman of Bengal)
  • Later known as Nur Jahan.
  • She was made official Badshah Begum.
  • She exercised tremendous influence over the state affairs.
  • Jahangir also issued silver coins in honour of his wife Mehr-un-Nissa.
  • He also married Manmati Bai (also known as Jagat Gosai) who was a Rathore princess. They gave birth to son Prince Khurram also known as "Shah Jahan".

Architecture during his Reign

  • The tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah, built by Nur Jahan in fond memory of her father, inlaid with Pietra Dura decoration is located in Agra.
  • The Sarai of Nurmahal is centrally protected monument of India, it is situated in Punjab constructed under the patronage of Nur Jahan.
  • Amar Singh of Mewar accepted the suzerainty of Jahangir.
  • In 1608 AD, he was visited by William Hawkins (a representative of British East India Company and was given Mansab of 400).
  • In 1615 AD, Sir Thomas Roe (an ambassador of King James I of England) came to his court.
  • Jahangir granted English to establish a port in Surat.
  • He captured a part of Ahmadnagar (Malik Amber ceded him the territory of Balaghat).
  • Shah Jahan and Mahabat Khan (commander) revolted against him.
  • He executed 5th Sikh Guru → Guru Arjan Dev because he gave refuge to Jahangir's son Khusrau.

He was buried in: Lahore.

Memoirs Written

  • Jahangir wrote his autobiography "Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri" in Persian language.

Biography

  • Matumid Khan wrote the biography of Jahangir known as "Iqbalnama-i-Jahangiri".

Shah Jahan (1628 AD–1658 AD)

  • Mother: Jagat Gosai (daughter of Raja Udai Singh).
  • He is best known for his Deccan and foreign policies.
  • Wife: Mumtaz Mahal.
  • Died in 1631, 3 yrs after Shahjahan's accession to the throne.
  • Original name: Arzumand Bano Begum.
  • Shah Jahan built Taj Mahal in her memory in Agra in 1632 AD-1653 AD (Ustad-Ahmad Lahori was the main architect of Taj Mahal).
  • 1632 AD, he defeated Portuguese.
  • In 1637 AD, he completely annexed Ahmadnagar.
  • His reign is described by:
  • French travellers Bernier (also a physician), Tavernier (he visited a total of 6 times) and Italian traveller Nicoli Mancci.
  • Bernier wrote: "Travels in the Mogul Empire".
  • Tavernier wrote: "Travels in India".
  • He introduced new administrative unit called Chakla.
  • Peter Mundi described famine that occured during his reign.
  • His reign is said to have marked Pinnacle of Mughal Dynasty.
  • He is known to have promoted art, culture, and architecture.

Architecture Built by Shah Jahan

Diwan-i-Aam (hall of public audience)

BuildersLocation
Akbar and later by Shah JahanAgra (Agra Fort)
Shah Jahan (when he shifted Capital from Agra to Delhi in 1638)Delhi (Red Fort)

Diwan-i-Khas (hall of private audience)

BuildersLocation

The Kohinoor and the Peacock Throne, both were stolen by Nadir Shah who invaded in 1739 AD.

Book

  • Padshahnama/Badshahnama written by Abdul Hamid Lahori during his reign.
  • In 1657 AD, his failing health set off the war of succession among his sons Dara Shikoh, Aurangzeb, Murad Baksh. In July 1658 AD, his son Aurangzeb emerged to be victorious.
  • Aurangzeb imprisoned his father in Agra Fort where he died in captivity in 1666 AD. He was buried at Taj Mahal (Agra) next to his wife Mumtaz's tomb.

Reason for Shah Jahan's imprisonment

  • Shah Jahan formally confirmed Dara Shikoh as his heir, granting him the title of Shahzada-e-Buland Iqbal ("Prince of High Fortune") and wanted him to ascend the throne.

Aurangzeb (1658 AD–1707 AD)

  • In 1658 AD, he defeated his elder brother Dara Shikoh (who was helped by Jaswanth Singh) at Dharmat (1658), Samugarh (1658), and Deorai (Varanasi).
  • After Victory: He was crowned at Delhi and assumed the title "Alamgir".
  • He captured Guru Teg Bahadur (9th Guru of Sikhs) and executed him because Guru Teg Bahadur refused to embrace Islam.
  • In 1686 AD, Bijapur was annexed by Aurangzeb.
  • In 1687 AD, he annexed Golconda.
  • He appointed "Muhtasibs" who were religious officers.
  • He wrote: Fatwa-i-Alamgiri (Muslim Laws).
  • He re-introduced Jaziya.
  • Death: 3 March 1707 AD at Bhingar (near Ahmednagar) — not at Daulatabad/Devgiri as is sometimes misstated.
  • Buried at: Khuldabad (Daulatabad).
  • He was called "Zinda Pir", the living saint.

Later Mughals

Bahadur Shah (1707 AD–1712 AD)

  • He is also known as Shah Alam I.

Later Mughals (continued)

Jahandar Shah (1712 AD–1713 AD)

  • He ascended to throne with the help of Zulfiqar Khan.
  • He abolished Jaziya.

Farrukh Siyar (1713 AD–1719 AD)

  • He ascended throne with the help of Sayyid Brothers (they were also known as King Makers): Hussain Ali Khan Barha and Abdullah Khan Barha.
  • He is known to issue "Golden Farman" to British East India Company.
  • Sayyid Brothers killed Farrukh Siyar with the help of Marathas (Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath).

Muhammad Shah (1719 AD–1748 AD)

  • He was also known as "Rangeela".
  • He killed the Sayyid Brothers with the help of Nizam-ul-Mulk.
  • During his reign Nadir Shah invaded. He sacked and plundered the city of Delhi in 1739 AD and took away immense amounts of wealth.
  • This invasion was followed by a series of plundering raids by the Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Abdali, who invaded north India five times between 1748 AD and 1761 AD.

Ahmed Shah (1748 AD–1754 AD)

Alamgir II (1754 AD–1759 AD)

  • He was also killed by nobles.

Shah Alam II (1759 AD–1806 AD)

  • He was blinded.

Akbar II (1806 AD–1837 AD)

Bahadur Shah II (1837 AD–1857 AD)

  • The last Mughal ruler.

Administration

  • Suba (lead by Subedar/Nizam) was divided into Sarkars (District) which was further divided into: Pargana (Taluka) and Gram (Village).
  • Siqdar (Revenue Officers) / Muqaddam (Village Headman)
  • Quanungo (Revenue Collector)

Important Officers

  • Mir Saman: In charge of Royal Household.
  • Mir Bakshi: Head of Military Department.
  • Diwan: Head of Revenue Administration.
  • Fauzdar: Maintained law and order.
  • Amalguzar: Responsible for assessment and collection of land revenue.
  • Sadr: Managed judicial affairs.
  • Shiqdar: Police Chief at Pargana level.
  • Amin: A revenue assessor at the Pargana level.

Rajputs

  • Many Rajput kings, particularly those belonging to Amber and Jodhpur, had served under the Mughals with distinction.
  • In exchange, they were permitted to enjoy considerable autonomy as Watan Jagirs.
  • These influential Rajput families claimed the subadari of rich provinces of Gujarat and Malwa.
  • Raja Ajit Singh of Jodhpur held the governorship of Gujarat and Sawai Raja Jai Singh II of Amber was the governor of Malwa.
  • Sawai Raja Jai Singh II founded his new capital at Jaipur and was given the Subadari of Agra in 1722 AD.

§ 4GOVERNORS-GENERAL (pre-1857)

The pre-1857 East India Company governors-general (and regulating-era figures).
Per T12 Bucket 3.3, this section was split out from
history/25 - Governor-General and Viceroy.md and appended here as the
closest administrative-history anchor (Mughal L2). New T01 L3:
history.mughal_empire.governors_general.

Lord Warren Hastings (1773-1785)

  • Regulating Act (1773) → 1st Governor General of Bengal.
  • Pitt's India Act (1784).
  • 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775-1782) → Treaty of Salbai signed (1782).
  • 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-1784).
  • Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784) formed.

Lord Cornwallis (1786-1793)

  • 3rd Anglo-Mysore War (1790-1792) → Treaty of Seringpatnam.
  • Permanent Settlement (1793).
  • Death: India (tomb in Ghazipur, Uttar Pradesh).
  • He is known as Father of Indian Civil Services.

Lord Wellesley (1798-1805)

  • 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-1805).
  • 4th Anglo-Mysore War (1799).
  • Treaty of Bassein (1802).

Lord Minto (1807-1813)

  • Treaty of Amritsar (1809) signed between Maharaja Ranjit Singh and Britishers.

Lord Hastings (1813-1823)

  • 3rd Anglo-Maratha War (1817-1819).
  • Anglo-Nepal War (1814-1816) → Treaty of Sugauli signed.
  • Ryotwari System introduced by Munro and Reed.

Lord William Bentinck (1828-1835)

  • First Governor-General of India.
  • Abolition of Sati (1829).
  • Suppression of Thugs.
  • He abolished Circuit Courts.
  • He is known as Father of Modern Education in India → Macaulay's Minute (1835) during his tenure.

Lord Metcalfe (1835-1836)

  • He is known as the Liberator of Indian Press.

Lord Auckland (1836-1842)

  • 1st Anglo-Afghan War (1838-1842).

Lord Hardinge I (1844-1848)

  • 1st Anglo-Sikh War → Treaty of Lahore signed.

Lord Dalhousie (1848-1856)

  • Doctrine of Lapse (1848).
  • 1st railway line laid down (1853) → from Bombay to Thane (34 km).
  • Widow Remarriage Act (1856).
  • Postal Act. Telegraph lines spread across.
  • Wood's Dispatch (1854) → Magna Carta of Indian Education.
  • He founded Public Works Department (PWD).
  • 2nd Anglo-Sikh War (1848-1849).
